title: Teaching begins at Baldwin Wallace and Princeton workshops
summary: Invited by Berger, Carter spent a week at Baldwin Wallace, then at Princeton, finding students knowledgeable about jazz.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Uh huh. But as things developed, of course, in the late 60's, you began a kind of a different type of date, playing at colleges and universities. I don't mean on a regular basis, but ...
Yes.
But you began to develop an interest in this kind of .. and also in teaching.
Yes.
Where did that begin?
Well, that began with an invitation from a gentleman from Princeton University, a Dr. Monroe Berger, whom I'm sure you've met.
Yes. Coming and going.

Coming and going, yes. And I hadn't met him, and I didn't know him, and he said if I was interested, he would come out to California at some future period and talk about it with me. And much to my surprise, he really came!

And we talked about it, and it wound up with my coming to Baldwin Wallace College, I believe that was in Middleburg, just outside of Cleveland. Berea, Ohio. And it seems that Mr., or Dr. Berger, who was doing these things, had been asked to come to Baldwin Wallace and he asked them if he could invite me. As a matter of fact, I don't know whether he made it one of the conditions or not, but I was very, very flattered and honored, and of course, quite pleased.
Was that the first time, then, that, you know, you spend the week there ...
Yes.
And then you played at some concerts; the Illinois Jazz Band with ...
Yes ... with John Garvey and his band came, yes.
And you would do a concert with them and you would do a concert with a trio from Cleveland.
Right.

Then you also met in workshops with students and talked with groups of students. Was that the first time that you had any extended contact -- extended at least, over a week's time ... with college students?
Yes. That was really I'd done anything of that nature, really.
Did you feel that that was something worthwhile doing? Was it an important thing to you? Was it some new dimension that you welcomed?
It was very, very new to me, of course, and very rewarding. I enjoyed it very much and it just really stimulated my interest in doing it more.
It was interesting also because students by and large were no longer jazz oriented; they were quite rock oriented at that time ...
Right.
Well how did ... you must have expected that, of course?

Well, I did expect it, but I was very pleased to see that the students, you know, that were getting in to their upper teens and beyond, were really getting much more interested -- and knowledgeable -- about jazz, you know? Which I found to be on a continued basis, even later, after I came to Princeton for a semester. And even after leaving Baldwin Wallace and coming to Princeton, I believe, for about a week or a couple of days here, ...
Right, and that was in early 1970?
Yes.
Directly after Baldwin Wallace.
Yes, that's right. After Baldwin Wallace. And it was very, very interesting -- the reaction of the students, and I guess I hadn't expected to find as much interest in jazz as I did.
You found more than you anticipated?
Yes, I think I did.
Well, did you find a knowledge of music that surprised you?
Oh, yes.
... that the kids were technically proficient?
Yes.
Even if the music was not jazz or if it was rock oriented?
Yes; they were being well schooled.

And of course when you came to Princeton, which was right after leaving Baldwin Wallace, we had a seminar with some jazz historians and critics of various times, including people like Dan Morganstern and Billy Taylor -- these were several that we did ...
Willie Ruff ...
Willie Ruff was here, Larry Ridley, and ...
Yes, that's right ... from Rutgers.
So this now became a combination of seminars, chats, workshops, and then concerts, all at the same time,
Yes, yes.
But this kind of variety -- did it prove for you to be particularly welcome?
Oh yes, indeed. Very.
